Preble Street
Good morning, Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and Members of the Veterans
and Legal Affairs Committee.
My name is Dan Hodgkins, and i am the Senior Director of Veterans Housing Services at
Preble Street and a chair of Maine's Homeless Veteran Action Committee (HVAC). Our Veterans Housing Services Program provides low-barrier, high-quality case management services to Veterans experiencing homelessness or at risk of homelessness across the
state. In FY25, we served 582 unduplicated veteran households across the entire state. Preble Street is a member of HVAC's No Homeless Veterans initiative, working in
partnership with over 20 other organizations to end Veteran homelessness in Maine.
I am here today to urge you to support LD 2135, An Act to Provide Funding to Keep Maine
Veterans Housed. This legislation represents a step forward in Maine's efforts to end Veteran homelessness through targeted support for best-practice landlord engagement
initiatives. A landlord incentive is a sum of money provided to a landlord who agrees to rent
to a tenant with limited rental history, a criminal record, or other barriers to housing, such as lived experience of homelessness Another incentive is access to a Risk Mitigation Fund
to reimburse landlords up to $1500 for unpaid rent or damage in excess of the security
deposit. These incentives allow case workers to quickly secure housing for homeless Veterans, as it separates them from other applicants in a competitive housing market.
Between April and September of last year, we housed 166 Veteran households. In 65 of those cases, we provided the landlord with an incentive, typically around $1,000, to lease
up a Veteran for at least one year. All of the homeless veterans that were leased up last year were covered by the Risk Mitigation Fund. Landlords appreciate these incentives, which
mitigate their risk and allow them to better support their community members; when another unit of theirs becomes available, they often call us first.
For "Tim," a 32-year-old Veteran, a landlord incentive was the difference between sleeping outside and having his own apartment. Tim was ready to start fresh, but his poor credit
history made landlords hesitant to rent to him. When Tim's caseworker offered a landlord
incentive, the landlord agreed to take a chance on him. Today, Tim remains stably housed and recently accepted a job that puts him over program income limits.
Radio ads are another best-practice landlord engagement strategy. These advertisements run on local radio stations, informing landlords about the benefits of renting to Veterans
experiencing homelessness and explaining how to get in touch. In the quarter before we ran

radio ads last year, we housed 47 Veterans. Once we started to run these ads, we were able to house 74 Veterans. Additionally, we saw a significant increase in website traffic and
received an average of 4 landlord inquiries per day. Additional funding through LD 2135 would support landlord engagement for housing homeless Veterans, a critical piece of
ending Veteran homelessness in Maine. We urge you to continue the state's progress
toward this goal by voting "Ought to Pass" on LD 2135.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
196563:
Testimony in Support of LD 2135
An Act to Provide Funding to Keep Maine Veterans Housed
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and distinguished members of the Veterans and
Legal Affairs Committee:
My name is David Patch, and I am the President of Maine Veterans in Need, a veteran-led, all
volunteer, nonprofit organization whose mission is to assist veterans and their dependents who
are in need, advocating for those in active crisis/emergency, preventing homelessness, helping
those who are homeless transition into stable housing, and prevent veteran suicide. I appreciate
the oppominity to testify today in strong support of LD 2135.
I want to be clear from the outset: This bill is not theoretical to me. This funding is not abstract. The problem it addresses is something l see every week, often every day, across Maine.
As President of Maine Veterans in Need, l work directly with homeless veterans, men and women who served our country and are now sleeping in their ears, living in tents in the woods, couch-surfing, or cycling through emergency shelters. Some are elderly. Some are disabled. Some are still working but cannot keep up with Maine's housing costs. Many are reluctant to ask
for help at all.
Veteran homelessness in Maine has improved over time, but it has not been solved. Recent Point-in-Time counts continue to identify well over one hundred veterans experiencing homelessness statewide in a single night, and those numbers do not always capture veterans
living in vehicles, encampments, or temporarily doubled up, whom my organization regularly
encounters. In practice, the need is larger and more persistent than the official counts suggest.
At the same time, Maine faces one of the tightest housing markets in the country. Rents continue to rise faster than fixed incomes, disability compensation, or entry-level wages. Even veterans
who qualify for federal housing assistance often struggle to find a landlord willing to accept
them, or to secure a unit before a crisis turns into homelessness.
This is where Preble Street's work is essential.
Preble Street is not just a service provider; it is a keystone organization in Maine's veteran homelessness response system. Their veteran housing staff conduct outreach, navigate complex systems, recruit landlords, and provide the practical supports that actually move veterans from
homelessness into housing.
Importantly, I can say from direct experience that the grant filnding referenced in LD 2135 has
worked.

Maine Veterans in Need has personally witnessed the positive impact of Preble Street's prior
fu11ding used for veteran housing efforts. Because of that funding:
- Veterans were able to secure apartments that otherwise would not have been available to
them. - Landlords were willing to take a chance on veterans with limited income or prior housing
instability.
- Housing placements happened faster, reducing time spent in shelters, vehicles, or cncampments.
o Veterans stabilized before their situations deteriorated into medical or mental health emergencies.
This is not just compassionate, it is cost-effective. Every veteran who is housed reduces the
burden on emergency rooms, law enforcement, shelters, and crisis services. Housing first and housing stabilization approaches consistently cost far less than allowing homelessness to persist.
Maine Veterans in Need does not replace Preble Street's work, we support and strengthen it.
MVN provides peer-based veteran engagement, emergency stabilization, benefits navigation, and
coordination across local and regional partners. Veterans often relate more easily to other
veterans, and that trust can be the key that opens the door to housing and services. When MVN
and Preble Street work together, outcomes improve.
LD 2135 recognizes an essential reality:
Ending veteran homelessness requires a coordinated system, not isolated efforts.
This $90,000 appropriation is modest in scale but high in impact. It helps replace lost grant funding so that proven strategies, landlord incentives, housing search support, and rapid
stabilization, do not disappear at a time when the housing market is already stacked against low-
income veterans.
I want to emphasize something important:
The veterans we serve are not asking for luxury. They are asking for safety, dignity, and stability.
A door that locks. A place to sleep. A chance to rebuild.
LD 2135 helps make that possible.
As someone who has sat with veterans in their cars in the winter, walked through encampments
in the woods, and helped people navigate the system one step at a time, I can say this with confidence: Preble Street's work saves lives, and this funding helps keep that work going.
On behalf of Maine Veterans in Need, and on behalf of the veterans We serve, I respectfully urge the committee to support LD 2135.
Thank you for your time, your service, and your commitment to Maine's veterans. I am happy to
answer any questions.

Testimony Neither for Nor Against:
L.D. 2135, "An Act to Provide Funding to Keep Maine Veterans Housed"
Ioint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and distinguished members of the Ioint Standing _ :_ __

Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs. I'm David Richmond, Director of the

Bureau. of

Veterans' Services (MBVS) and I'm here today to testify neither for nor against L.D. 2135, "An Act

to Provide Funding to Keep Maine Veterans" .

LD 2185 proposes a one-time General Fund appropriation to support housing stabilization
activities for veterans through Preble Street, including landlord incentives, outreach, and the resolution of past rental debts. The intent of the bill aligns with ongoing statewide and federal efforts to reduce veteran homelessness and maintain access to permanent `supportive housing.

The Maine Bureau of Veterans' Services recognizes and values the important Work that Preble
Street performs in serving homeless veterans in our state. Their organization is a key partner within Maine's broader continuum of care and has contributed meaningfully to efforts to stabilize
housing for vulnerable veteran populations.

However, MBVS would like to share several considerations related to the proposed funding
structure. As a state agency, any disbursement of General Fund monies, even on a one-time basis, would be subject to state procurement statutes, fiscal policies, and oversight requirements. This would necessitate the establislunent of rules, monitoring mechanisms, and accountability
structures to ensure appropriate use of state funds. These requirements may limit the flexibility
intended by the proposal, particularly for funding designed to incentivize landlords and respond
quickly to housing-related needs.

Additionally, while Preble Street is an important partner, it represents one organization within a
larger network of service providers working to address veteran homelessness across Maine. Many
of these organizations were similarly impacted by the loss of federal funding. Directing state
funds to a single provider may raise equity considerations when other organizations are
performing comparable work in different regions of the state.

MBVS remains committed to working collaboratively with the Legislature, state agencies, and
community partners to explore solutions that are equitable, fiscally responsible, and aligned with state procurement requirements, while continuing to support efforts to prevent and reduce
veteran homelessness.
Thank you for your consideration. I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.
Respectfully Submitted,
David Richmond Director, Maine Bureau of Veterans' Services

Testimony of Senator Tim Nangle introducing
LD 2135, "An Act to Provide Funding to Keep Maine Veterans Housed,"
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs January 21, 2026
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee
on Veterans and Legal Affairs, I am Senator Tim Nangle. I represent Senate District 26, which
includes the communities of Windham, Raymond, Casco, Frye Island, and part of Westbrook. Thank
you for the opportunity to present LD 2135, "An Act to Provide Funding to Keep Maine Veterans
Housed."
As I'm sure this committee knows, too many veterans who have served our country with honor are still struggling to find and keep stable housing. At a time when federal programs are being cut or delayed across the country, it is more important than ever that we strengthen the local partnerships that are
already working. This bill is intended to ensure that Maine veterans can continue to count on proven supports that help keep them housed and comiected to their communities.
LD 2135 would provide support to the Veterans Flex Fund -- an already successful program led by
Preble Street and the Maine Homeless Veterans Action Committee, which includes the 'U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, the Maine Bureau of Veterans Services, Volunteers of America, Vets Inc., Bread of Life Ministries, and others.
The program provides small but critical assistance to help veterans overcome barriers to stable housing, such as covering unexpected rental costs, offering incentives to landlords, and conducting outreach to connect veterans with safe, affordable homes. The Veterans Flex fund is currently supported by a grant that is nearly exhausted. This bill proposes a modest, one-time appropriation to help keep the Flex Fund in place while that broader coalition continues its work. It is a short-term
solution, but one with immediate, real-life benefits for veterans who are at risk right now.
More broadly, I hope this bill becomes part of a larger conversation on the role the Legislature should
play in supporting flexible, coordinated approaches like this into the future -- approaches that have
shown results and help ensure that veterans do not lose housing due to gaps we have the power to
address.
LD 2135 is a practical step to make sure that veterans do not lose housing simply because a proven
tool ran out of funding. It allows work that is already underway to continue and helps ensure that the
progress we have made does not slip backward.
Thank you for your time, and I would be happy to answer any questions. I also understand there are
folks here from Preble Street who can answer more specific questions about the program.
